note_claims.claim: The patient is presenting with worsening exertional breathlessness and COPD.
The patient has MRC dyspnoea grade 3.
The patient has a morning cough with white sputum.
The patient has had two exacerbations requiring oral steroids in the last 5 years.
One of the exacerbations required antibiotics.
The patient has no history of hospital admissions.
The patient has no ankle swelling.
The patient has no chest pain, haemoptysis, or weight loss.
The patient is an ex-smoker for 6 months.
The patient has approximately 30 pack-years of smoking history.
The patient is prescribed Anoro Ellipta (umeclidinium/vilanterol) one inhalation once daily.
The patient is prescribed Salbutamol as needed (about twice daily).
The patient has no known drug allergies.
The patient's oxygen level is 93 percent on air.
The patient's breathing rate is 20.
The patient has bilateral wheeze.
The patient has coarse crackles at the bottom of the left lung, at the left base (new finding).
The patient's FEV1 is 52 percent of predicted, which is lower than last year.
The patient's blood eosinophil count last month was 0.35 × 10⁹/L.
The patient has COPD with frequent exacerbations despite LAMA/LABA.
The patient's eosinophil count (0.35) is ≥0.3, making them suitable for triple therapy.
There are new focal crackles at the left base.
The plan is to switch the patient from Anoro to Trelegy Ellipta one inhalation once daily.
Pulmonary rehabilitation is offered but declined by the patient.
A chest X-ray is ordered today.
The patient is scheduled for a clinic review in three months.
The patient should contact their GP the same day if there is increased breathlessness, sputum volume, or a change in sputum colour.
The patient should call 999 if they are very breathless.

transcript_facts.fact: The clinician is Dr Nwosu from the respiratory team.
The patient's wife is Valerie.
The patient reports being more breathless and having to stop halfway up the hill to the shops.
The patient can walk on the flat at their own pace, but is slower than Valerie.
The patient has a cough most mornings with white phlegm.
The patient has had two flare-ups: one in January and one in the summer.
Both flare-ups required antibiotics, specifically the summer one.
The patient has no hospital admissions.
The relative is the one with the swollen ankles, and the patient's are fine.
The clinician asks about chest pain or coughing up blood.
The patient reports no chest pain or coughing up blood.
The clinician asks if the patient stopped smoking.
The patient stopped smoking six months ago and has not smoked since.
The clinician asks how much and for how long the patient smoked.
The patient smoked twenty cigarettes a day for forty years, stopping for ten years in the middle, resulting in thirty years of smoking.
The clinician asks what inhalers the patient is using.
The patient is using the Anoro inhaler once a day and the blue inhaler maybe twice a day.
The patient has no known drug allergies, only the inhalers.
The clinician notes the patient's oxygen level is 93 percent on air and breathing rate is 20.
The clinician notes there is some wheeze on both sides and some coarse crackles at the bottom of the left lung, at the left base.
The patient asks if the crackles are new.
The clinician states the crackles were not noted last time.
The patient's breathing test shows an FEV1 of 52 percent of predicted, which is a bit lower than last year.
The patient's blood eosinophil count last month was 0.35.
The clinician advises contacting the GP the same day if there is increased breathlessness, sputum volume, or a change in sputum colour.
The clinician advises calling 999 if the patient is very breathless.
